item.title: Maher blasts Rand Paul for releasing Fauci’s COVID diaries as PR expert suggests a new course for the Senator
item.description: Comedian Bill Maher accused Rand Paul of betraying his libertarian brand by releasing Fauci's private COVID-19 diary and pursuing contempt charges.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher is taking aim at Sen. Rand Paul for what the host says betrays Paul's own brand.

During Friday's episode of HBO's "Real Time," Maher accused Paul, R-Ky., of breaking with his libertarian views by releasing Fauci's pandemic-era diary and threatening to hold him in contempt of Congress. Meanwhile, a public relations expert told Fox News Digital that Paul should focus on why the diary matters rather than how he obtained it.

"Stop threatening to put everyone in jail who you just don’t like," Maher said more broadly about politics. 

"Rand, babe, your entire brand is ‘Senator Right to Privacy,’" he added. "You’re the libertarian guy, the Fourth Amendment guy. It’s your family legacy."

BILL MAHER BREAKS WITH THE LEFT TO HAMMER ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER EXPLOSIVE SENATE HEARING

Maher’s comments come on the heels of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which is led by Paul, voting 8-5 to refer Fauci for contempt after he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Senate hearing regarding his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic last week.

Fauci, who received a preemptive pardon from then-President Joe Biden last year, exercised his right against self-incrimination a total of 111 times during the hearing while being questioned over his leadership as the White House chief medical adviser during the pandemic.

In the days before the hearing, Paul released more than 1000 pages of Fauci's private "COVID diaries" — medical notes and personal reflections Fauci wrote and stored on his government computer.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The move was blasted by Maher, who argued Paul's decision to publish the documents directly contradicted his longtime political platform of personal privacy and limited government intrusion.

"Your entire political career has been about warning us about government overreach," Maher said, speaking directly to Paul. "You printing someone's diary? It's like [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez] wearing a gown that says, ‘Tax the poor.’"

Fauci's diaries were located and stored on government servers. 

Jason Mudd, CEO of Axia Public Relations, told Fox News Digital that the criticism surrounding Paul's release of Fauci's private diary is unfounded, while adding he would advise Paul to change approach to explaining why the document is important.

"If Sen. Paul were my client, I’d tell him to stop defending how he got the diary and start defending why it matters," Mudd said. "A public official’s notes on a government computer aren’t a private citizen’s journal, and that distinction should have been his first sentence, not his fifth."  

Maher’s comments come after he previously made headlines by suggesting that his "vote is in play" after voicing his discontent with the socialist direction the Democratic party is heading.

"Politically, Bill Maher carries resonance with a fairly non-tribal group of viewers. While that means he can often piss off both sides, it also means he can be seen as above the partisan back-and-forth, without a specific left or right agenda," media expert Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital.

DAVID MARCUS: BILL MAHER'S NO REPUBLICAN, HE'S JUST A RARE DEMOCRAT WHO THINKS

Shroff added that Maher's words carry more weight when he criticizes both sides of the political spectrum because of his willingness to call out his own party.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Maher can spend one week arguing that Democrats have lost the plot and the next saying Republicans have gone too far," Shroff said. "That gives moments like this outsized significance: when someone who has repeatedly criticized Fauci and the left still looks at what Rand Paul is doing and says it crosses a line, it gives permission to viewers who aren’t particularly sympathetic to Fauci to reach the same conclusion."

"In a polarized media environment, the messenger can matter as much as the message," Shroff added. 

Fox News Digital reached out to Senator Paul and Dr. Fauci for comment.

item.title: Joe Biden's cancer has spread further, leaving him in 'very painful' condition, Hunter reveals
item.description: Hunter Biden told the BBC that his father's prostate cancer has metastasized into his bones, calling it "very painful" and "very debilitating."
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him significant pain, his son Hunter Biden revealed during a Friday interview.

"The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," Hunter Biden told the BBC in an interview which aired Friday. "It’s very painful and it’s very debilitating in many respects," he added.

"It’s really sad to watch," Hunter Biden said. "The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good."

Despite his poor health, Hunter Biden said his father is "still doing his thing," and attending speaking engagements.

HUNTER BIDEN CLAIMS UNDER OATH THAT HIS FAMILY IS BROKE AMID FIGHT OVER $17M LEGAL BILL

Joe Biden revealed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, just months after he departed the Oval Office.

The diagnosis at the time was that the cancer was Stage 4, "aggressive" and had already spread to his bones.

He received a Gleason score of 9, indicating both the cancer's aggressive nature and the potential that he had been living with it for years.

WATCH: WOULD-BE SECOND-TERM PRESIDENT BIDEN LEFT SEARCHING FOR FAMILY ON STAGE AFTER OBAMA CENTER OPENING

"He had it while he was president," said Dr. Ezekiel J. Emanuel, vice provost and oncologist at the University of Pennsylvania, adding Joe Biden "probably had it at the start of his presidency in 2021."

"He did not develop it in the last 100 to 200 days," Emanuel said, according to the American Journal of Medical Care.

Joe Biden's wife, Jill, previously told the hosts of ABC's "The View" that his cancer has slowed him down.

"He keeps his schedule, but he’s slowed down," she said in June. "I mean, stage four cancer is — and he's 83 — so, I think the mix of everything and the medications that he's taken has made life a little more difficult these days."

Fox News Digital contacted the Office of Joe and Jill Biden for further comment.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

item.title: Florida business owners allegedly scattered 1,500 mothballs on beach to send endangered birds packing
item.description: Two St. Pete Beach business owners allegedly spread 1,500 toxic mothballs on sand to stop black skimmers from nesting, now facing felony charges.
item.content:encoded:
Two Florida business owners have been charged with third-degree felonies after allegedly spreading about 1,500 "toxic" mothballs across a beach in hopes of keeping an "imperiled" bird species from nesting there.

If convicted, they could each face up to five years in prison, fines of up to $5,000 and up to five years of probation.

The problem started in late April when beachgoers noticed mothballs on the white, sugary sand on St. Pete Beach in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) and bird-loving volunteers from the Audubon Society mobilized. They plucked about 1,000 of the small, white orbs from the sand behind the Plaza Beach Hotel.

MASSACHUSETTS HOMEOWNERS STUNNED AFTER TOWN WARNS JULY 4 FLAGS THREATEN ENDANGERED BIRDS

Then 500 more appeared overnight.

The smelly balls containing pesticides dotted an area where endangered shorebirds known as black skimmers were "attempting to establish a nesting colony," FWC officials said in a news conference. Their placement also meant other wildlife and children "could easily come in contact with them."

It quickly became clear that someone might be targeting the birds, they said.

So FWC investigators flew into action.

Meanwhile, the discovery of the mothballs ruffled feathers in the community.

There was "a lot of public outcry" expressing concern for the birds, while investigators tried to locate the source of the mothballs, FWC officials said.

Law enforcement served search warrants, combed through "terabytes" of data and eventually seized cellphones to try to locate the individuals behind the caper.

That work led them to Christopher Monroe, owner and manager of Chris’s Beachside Bar, and Robert Czyszczon, owner of the Plaza Beach Hotel, FWC officials said.

Out of fear of lost revenue, the two allegedly hatched a plan to use mothballs to deter birds from congregating on the beach behind their businesses, authorities said.

HIKERS FACE $25,000 FINE AFTER OFF-LEASH DOG BARKED AT GRIZZLY BEAR ON BANFF NATIONAL PARK TRAIL

Through video surveillance and receipt records, investigators found that Czyszczon spent about $60 buying "a large quantity" of mothballs at a Walmart the day before they first appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

Upon examining his phone, investigators found "incriminating" text messages between him and fellow business owner, Monroe, discussing their objections to the native fowl.

Text conversations revealed plans for placement of the mothballs on the beach, officials said. That’s what led investigators to Monroe as a suspect.

The men discussed how they "were going to do something" to prevent the birds from nesting on the beach, FWC officials said.

Black skimmers don’t nest in trees. They kick beach sand backwards to make depressions on the ground. Then they lay their eggs and raise their young near the surf.

"They're the worst birds," one of the men allegedly wrote in anticipation of nesting season.

"The bird people will put up fence around the area, and then the beach people will not be able to get to and from because they will fence around that space."

Cellphone tower data showed Monroe’s phone was at the same location as Czyszczon’s phone on both nights when the mothballs appeared on the beach, FWC officials said.

The men feared that nests on the beach would lead to fewer customers and less money being spent there, authorities said.

"Why didn't you tell me we lose $25,000 to $50,000?" one allegedly wrote in a text.

Monroe and Czyszczon were charged with illegal dumping, a third-degree felony, according to Pinellas County court records. They also were charged with the "attempted take of a state-listed imperiled species by harassment," a misdemeanor, according to FWC officials.

Both are out of jail on bond.

MASSACHUSETTS HOMEOWNERS STUNNED AFTER TOWN WARNS JULY 4 FLAGS THREATEN ENDANGERED BIRDS

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

About 6,800 black skimmers live in Florida. FWC officials estimate that several hundred live on the beaches of Pinellas County.

SEND US A TIP

The pesticide in mothballs can harm people and wildlife that come into contact with their vapors, according to an educational publication by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (IFAS).

"With any pesticide, the label is the law," Brett W. Bultemeier, director of the UF/IFAS Pesticide Information Office, wrote in a 2021 educational publication about mothballs. "The label language is not simply a set of directions. Rather, they are requirements that are legally enforceable."

GOT A TIP?

The birds probably weren’t hurt by the "harassment," FWC officials said.

But it did delay their nesting, they said. That pushes the date that their young can fledge from the nest further back in the season. And that could put them in danger.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

A big storm at the end of hurricane season, which ends on Nov. 30, "can wipe out a colony if those young birds haven't fledged yet," an FWC official said.

An attorney for Czyszczon did not respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital. Court records indicate that Monroe doesn’t have an attorney. He couldn’t be reached for comment.

item.title: Cornell bans bear butchering after students carved up creature in dorm kitchen
item.description: Cornell University now bans wild game processing in dorm kitchens after two students went viral for butchering a black bear in Ganędagǫ Hall.
item.content:encoded:
Cornell University has added a new rule banning the processing of wild game in school kitchens months after two students went viral for carving up a bear in a dormitory kitchen.

"Processing wild/game animals in community kitchens is strictly prohibited," the school's new policy reads.

The school confirmed to a student newspaper that the rule's addition was a direct response to the 2025 incident, which saw two students drag the carcass of a black bear they had killed into Cornell's Ganędagǫ Hall for preparation.

One of those students, Aaron Chin, revealed himself as one of the butchers on a podcast a few months after the incident.

CODY JOHNSON FIRES BACK AT CRITICS, CALLS ALASKA GRIZZLY BEAR HUNT A 'CONSERVATIONIST EFFORT'

Chin explained that he and his hunting partner, a fellow Cornell student, had planned on bringing the bear from the hunting grounds located roughly two hours from the school to a friend's house to prepare it, but claimed the friend had an emergency that left them unable to use his home.

Chin also said that before bringing the bear meat on campus, he and his partner ensured they weren't breaking any campus rules.

"We were really diligent in reading all of the rules [and] regulations," Chin told the MeatEater podcast in September. "We made sure we did everything by the book because we knew we were going to be under scrutiny."

The incident incurred swift social media and on-campus backlash, prompting state regulators to investigate.

However, after an inspector from New York's Department of Environmental Conservation visited the kitchen where the carving took place, the agency found no code violations, according to an NBC report.

item.title: White Sox manager Will Venable forgets key rule in inexplicable blunder, costs team in loss
item.description: Will Venable forgot a key mound visit rule, forcing Noah Schultz out after just five batters and taxing an already exhausted Chicago White Sox bullpen.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable has done a tremendous job in his first season with the club, with many fine moments throughout the season.

However, in the White Sox’s 8-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians at Rate Field on Friday, Venable did not have one of his finer moments, as he forgot a key rule and cost his team dearly.

Just four batters into the game, White Sox starting pitcher Noah Schultz had loaded the bases, drawing a mound visit from pitching coach Zach Bove. One batter later, left fielder Angel Martinez ripped a two-run single.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Venable then went to the mound to talk about an appeal play but forgot that he wasn’t allowed to do so.

Under official rule 5.10(l), "a manager or coach is allowed only one visit to the mound per pitcher in a single inning without penalty. If the same coach or manager makes a second visit to the same pitcher in the same inning, the pitcher must be removed from the pitching position."

Venable’s visit to the mound meant that he had to remove Schultz from the game just five batters in. His gaffe was especially costly, because the team lost in 13 innings the night before and taxed its bullpen.

Venable’s blunder meant that his already taxed bullpen was going to have to work 8 2/3 innings. David Sandlin, who replaced Schultz, hadn’t even begun throwing in the bullpen when Venable went to the pitcher’s mound; he was just getting loose and stretching.

While Venable said after the game that Schultz was not going to pitch long in the game anyway, he certainly would have lasted more than the five batters he faced if it weren't for Venable's mound visit. The 43-year-old manager took full responsibility for his error.

"Yeah, just an inexcusable mistake by me where we had an appeal play that we wanted to execute, and in the urgency of trying to make that happen, just totally lost that we had visited," Venable said, according to MLB.com. "Obviously that was a mistake. So, just messed it up."

Sandlin, who was callup from Triple-A before the game, ended saving the bullpen, as he pitched 5 1/3 innings on 96 pitches. While the circumstances of his entering the game were odd, he didn’t make any excuses.

"I got a little extra time out there," Sandlin said. "I think I got about eight pitches in the 'pen and then got to warm up out there. Can't make any excuses, just have to get going. Felt good enough and started off great."

For the White Sox, it was their fourth straight loss, making them the last team in baseball to have a four-game losing streak this season. They had not lost more than three in a row before Friday.

item.title: Jamie Kennedy blasts left-wing double standards following 'maggot' attacks
item.description: Jamie Kennedy says he's labeled a "maggot" for supporting Trump policies and slams the left as fake on inclusion during a fiery podcast episode.
item.content:encoded:
Jamie Kennedy is calling out what he sees as hypocrisy in America today.

The actor released a solo episode of his podcast, "Hate to Break It to Ya," this week, and spoke at length about current events, namely the Fauci hearings and the renewed conversation around the COVID-19 pandemic and its lasting effects.

During the episode, Kennedy's discussion of the public response to the pandemic became a bit broader when he spoke about some people today being "beyond brainwashed."

JAMIE KENNEDY BLASTS MARK HAMILL'S DEAD TRUMP POST AS 'EVIL' AFTER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

"And I've never seen this in the history of our race of human beings," he continued. "For instance, if I like something that a Republican does, or Trump does, they call me not just MAGA, they call me a maggot. A maggot."

He explained that while he does lean right, he "never even voted," and he said there are some more liberal policies he agrees with as well, "but if I say I like that Trump secures the borders, I'm just a maggot."

The "Scream" star said he believes that people like him, who focus on policy over party, are "open-minded," while people on the left have "no leniency."

"How can you say that you're the party of inclusion when you don't include us?" he asked. "All we want to do is talk to people, figure out things, go through different ideas, see what we like. And if we don't, we don't feel like we've looked under every stone. And I feel like that's what's happening – people don't want you to investigate. If you even investigate or go against their beliefs, they just put you in a box."

Kennedy also spoke about performing an hour-long comedy set in a parking lot to raise money for a bar that had been struggling to stay afloat under lockdown restrictions. The event was nearly shut down while, at the same time, he claimed, a crew of dozens was shooting a television show in another parking lot nearby with no issues because it had been "sanctioned by the state."

"That's the hypocrisy," he complained. "A female, family-owned business, probably very left-leaning ... and you've turned them into me. And you know what you think I am."

He continued, "So when you say that people are like this, it's because you're so repressive. You're so judgmental, you're so mean. You're so arrogant, you're so impatient, you're so ... there's nothing sweet about you. There's nothing open or forgiving."

"The reason why no one believes your bulls— when you're this wild, angry, crazy left-leaning person ... is that the right-leaning people, if they say hateful things, they kind of stand by it," Kennedy said, claiming that if someone on the right holds "hateful" beliefs, "at least you know where you stand with them."

"If you're a wild leftist, your whole thing is inclusion," he argued, and "the minute they don't get what they want," they turn into a "gremlin-possessed demon."

"Why we don't listen to you is because we don't believe a word you say," he went on, "because you're all words. You're nothing but ... you're air. You're not a really good person, you're fake. We all know it. People like me know it. There's tons of people like me – we know it."

As another example, Kennedy brought up the murder of Charlie Kirk, saying that "if you're an empathetic person, you were f—ing ruined for a week. I don't care what you are – if you're a human, and you have blood in your veins and love in your heart, you don't wish what happened to him on anyone."

But the people who celebrated Kirk's death, he said, are "beyond sick, and we saw how many people did that."

"These are the people that want all the inclusion and say that we're not," he said. "No, we just know your bulls—. You just want what you want, and if you don't get it, 'it's my ball, and my that, I'm going home,' but you don't just go home, you burn ours down. You're not just crybabies, you're psychopaths."

"You talk about a cult," he said later. "The cult of closed-mindedness. That's what it is."

item.title: Philadelphia Eagles 2026 outlook: Why betting on them to miss the playoffs has real value
item.description: The Philadelphia Eagles added Riq Woolen and Jonathan Greenard on defense, but questions about Jalen Hurts and a tougher division loom large.
item.content:encoded:
It is crazy just how much can change from one year to the next, especially in the NFL. We know there are going to be good teams that seem to succeed every year. Sometimes, though, there are teams that are good, but almost seem like they are fake good. That’s what I thought of the Eagles last year. Are they going to be good, bad, or somewhere in between this season?

The Eagles did make the playoffs a year after winning the Super Bowl over the Chiefs with ease. The team was just 11-6 for the season, though. The Eagles started the year looking dominant once again, winning all of their first four games. Then they had a tough home loss to Denver and an embarrassing road loss to the Giants. They won another four before they slumped to another three straight losses against the Cowboys, the Bears, and Chargers. The last week of the season meant nothing, and they lost to the Commanders. Of their six regular season losses, three were to non-playoff teams. In the postseason, they were in a back-and-forth battle with the 49ers before they lost in the fourth quarter.

A.J. BROWN HEADED TO NEW ENGLAND TO REUNITE WITH MIKE VRABEL AFTER A SEASON OF EAGLES UNHAPPINESS

item.title: Couples asking wedding guests for cash spark fierce debate over manners and tradition
item.description: AnnaLynne McCord and Danny Cipriani's Honeyfund wedding registry sparks a heated debate over whether asking guests for cash is tacky or modern.
item.content:encoded:
A celebrity couple asking wedding guests to help fund their nuptials is being branded "tacky" by some, while others insist cash is king.

American actress AnnaLynne McCord, known for her roles on "90210," "Nip/Tuck" and "Days of Our Lives," and her English former professional rugby player fiancé, Danny Cipriani, set up a page on Honeyfund, an online wedding and honeymoon registry, inviting people to contribute to wish-list elements of their "dream wedding."

The registry lists wedding expenses ranging from $100 to $600, including the marriage license, reception beverages, photography, rehearsal dinner and floral arrangements.

"Tacky is an ugly word, but it’s really unkind to ask your guests to give you money for any occasion," Texas-based etiquette expert Diane Gottsman told Fox News Digital. "It really is impolite to straight out ask for cash. You let your family do the talking for you. You let your website do the talking for you."

Gottsman said every couple needs a registry to give options for guests, but asking directly for cash sets the wrong tone immediately.

Cash is easy to give, she added, and is acceptable to include as a request on a website for honeymoon funds, a down payment for a home, etc., but it shouldn’t be the only option. Some guests prefer to give a gift, and it should be left up to them.

"A gift is not an admission ticket to your wedding," Gottsman said. "A registry makes it easier, but guests can do whatever they would like. It’s a gracious act of giving that they’re doing for you."

Several Reddit discussions about cash wedding registries suggest attitudes vary, with some users saying the practice is a modern, accepted trend. Gottsman clarified that a cash option is perfectly acceptable, but asking guests to pay for the wedding itself is "off-putting."

One Reddit forum asked, "Is it bad to ask for money instead of gifts?"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"No, most people do this now, majority of weddings I’ve been to the last few years all were mainly cash registries," one user replied.

"We did, and didn’t get any backlash and got money from everyone, except one friend who offered us either money or getting a meat subscription box," another user responded. "And we love to cook and good meat is dang expensive so we took it, but we didn’t get any surprise gifts from people who refused to give us cash or anything like that."

A Redditor identifying as an Asian person said the only gift you give or receive in that culture is money.

"Can someone please explain to me why it is such a ‘bad’ thing to not have a physical registry? Like I don’t get it," the person wrote. "If I want something, you giving me the money will let me buy it. If I already have everything I need, money can help re-coop the cost of the wedding or literally anything else. Money is the best, most versatile gift."

"Why in American culture is it seen so negatively?" the person added. "I’m born and raised in the U.S., and I still never understood people’s issue with this."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It’s a general taboo around money in American culture," a fellow Redditor replied. "You’re not supposed to talk about money at all honestly. So asking for it or exchanging it directly is frowned upon. That’s why there’s such a culture around signaling wealth indirectly. Having a big wedding or designer bags is how to flaunt wealth, not posting a screenshot of your bank statement."

Someone else on Reddit asked if it would be rude to ask for money instead of gifts for her wedding, then edited the original post to say she decided against it and to include cash as an option among other gifts on her registry.

"Just have a honeymoon fund and few or no physical items on your registry and most people will take the hint," someone on the forum advised.

Gottsman encouraged couples to "think about the ask." They should throw a wedding they can afford, because asking for cash sets a different tone for the celebration.

If a guest is reluctant to chip in on a couple’s wedding, Gottsman said there’s a gracious way to decline.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Say, ‘I have something else in mind, and I’m really hoping you enjoy it,’ not, ‘I’m not giving you cash, because it annoys me,’" she said.

A timeless, go-to gift for a couple is something sentimental and thoughtful that you know the couple will like. If you don’t have any ideas, give them something they can return. Make sure you are always including a gift receipt, Gottsman said.

item.title: Hawaii voters hit the polls as Gov. Josh Green dominates, progressive takes aim at Dem congressman
item.description: Hawaii's 1st Congressional District primary pits Rep. Ed Case against Jarrett Keohokalole, who opposes Donald Trump tariffs and ICE enforcement.
item.content:encoded:
Hawaii voters will decide Saturday who advances to the November general election, with key contests including the race for governor and the battle to represent the state’s 1st Congressional District.

Gov. Josh Green, who was first elected in 2022, is heavily favored to win the Democratic primary, where he faces three little-known competitors. His challengers include George "Teva" Lucas-Tadeo, a Democratic socialist who has promised on social media to open a government-run grocery store and legalize recreational marijuana.

David "Duke" Bourgoin is mounting his second primary challenge against Green after losing to him in 2022, when he captured only 590 votes against Green’s 158,161. He also lost two bids for Honolulu mayor, in 2022 and 2024.

JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN

Lauren Kapoliahiʻiaka Shim is also seeking the Democratic nomination. She is the CEO and founder of Aloha AI Incorporated, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Neither Lucas-Tadeo nor Shim had campaign websites, and none of Green’s three challengers had raised any money in the race as of June 30, according to Honolulu Civil Beat. Meanwhile, Green has raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Republican Gary Cordery, the race’s second-highest fundraiser, who has raised about $313,000, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Cordery, owner of the contracting company Kingdom Builders, and Ken Fujiyama, an entrepreneur and investor, are competing for the Republican nomination and a chance to end nearly two decades of Democratic control of the governor’s mansion. The last Republican to serve as Hawaii governor was Linda Lingle, who held the office from 2002 to 2010.

Cordery has campaigned on lowering Hawaii’s high cost of living, expanding housing and cracking down on government waste and corruption. He has proposed adding 15,000 homes for working families, using state-owned land for housing and eliminating the state’s general excise tax on food and medicine. Fujiyama has also proposed a plan to tackle the housing affordability crisis by developing 100,000 residential lots and partnering with large landowners to spur growth.

MICHIGAN’S TOP ELECTION OFFICIAL WINS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR, ADVANCES TO BATTLEGROUND RACE

Whoever emerges from the Republican primary will face an uphill battle to unseat Green if he secures the Democratic nomination. Green holds a 56% approval rating, while the Cook Political Report rates the race "Likely Democrat" and gives Democrats a 13-point advantage.

Meanwhile, eyes outside of Hawaii will be locked on the Democratic primary in the 1st Congressional District, where state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole is challenging Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii.

Case, who is seeking a seventh term, has represented the district since 2019 and argues that his seniority and position on the Appropriations Committee give Hawaii greater influence in Washington. Meanwhile, Keohokalole, who is endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders' group Our Revolution, is running on a progressive platform that includes Medicare for All and opposition to ICE and President Donald Trump's tariffs.

Keohokalole is seeking to portray Case as out of touch with Democratic voters, pointing to the congressman’s vote with House Republicans to pass Trump's SAVE America Act, which would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

Given the district’s strong Democratic lean, whoever wins the party’s primary will likely be favored to win the seat in November.

Polls close at 7pm local time.

item.title: 'Remember the Titans' star Ethan Suplee says one hard truth fueled his 300-pound weight loss
item.description: Ethan Suplee reveals how treating weight loss like his sobriety helped him maintain a 300-pound transformation after years of failed attempts.
item.content:encoded:
"Remember the Titans" star Ethan Suplee spent years dramatically transforming his body, but the actor says the breakthrough that finally helped him maintain his weight loss came when he stopped viewing it as something he could permanently "cure."

Suplee explained he saw the biggest change when he began treating his relationship with food and weight much like his sobriety — a lifelong condition requiring honesty, communication and accountability.

Reflecting on his recovery journey with Fox News Digital, Suplee said repeated attempts to get sober failed because he believed he could simply complete rehab and move on. He believed taking 30 days away from drugs and alcohol meant the problem had gone away.

"I haven’t had drugs or alcohol in 30 days," he recalled. "That means I’m cured."

'REMEMBER THE TITANS' STAR ETHAN SUPLEE ISSUES WARNING ABOUT WEIGHT LOSS DRUG CRAZE

It wasn't until he embraced ongoing accountability and open communication that he found lasting success, a lesson he later realized applied just as much to maintaining his weight loss.

"My condition isn’t a condition with a cure," Suplee explained. "It’s a condition that I can learn to manage."

He added, "I did not apply that to weight loss for many, many years. I kind of was doing everything in my head, and the big boon to actually being able to maintain it was finding a group of people to be accountable to."

CELEBRITY CHEF REVEALS NO. 1 MISTAKE SABOTAGING YOUR WEIGHT LOSS: 'FUZZY MATH'

Suplee has been candid about his decades-long battle with obesity. The "My Name is Earl" actor weighed roughly 500 pounds at his heaviest and ultimately lost around 300 pounds through years of diet and lifestyle changes. He has also undergone multiple skin-removal surgeries and now hosts weekly discussions on his show, "LifeLONG with Ethan Suplee," about long-term weight management.

"There’s some pressure from the world to continue to manage [the weight loss]," he told Fox News Digital. "But that’s something I’ve kind of designed."

On his weekly live show and podcast, "LifeLONG," Suplee regularly discusses the realities of long-term weight maintenance, inviting experts and people who have transformed their health to talk about nutrition, emotional eating, fitness and accountability. The show's central message is that health is an ongoing practice — not a destination.

"It’s a group of people, like-minded people, who come in, and we share what we’re going through, and we share our experience," Suplee explained. "And I think we all do better because of that."

After decades of trial and error, Suplee said his own experience taught him there is no shortcut to lasting weight loss. While he acknowledged that weight-loss drugs can be an effective tool, he argued they aren't a replacement for building healthier habits.

"As a kid, I wanted a magical diet drug so badly. And now we have what is a magical diet drug," he said. "I think, unfortunately, it's also not a one-stop shop. I think you can hop on a GLP-1 and experience weight loss. You can see the scale go down week over week for a long time without having to do anything else."

"... I think when people imagine their ideal – I don't think the GLP-1s get anyone to their ideal."

Suplee said his own experience ultimately shaped a simple philosophy: There's no single answer when it comes to long-term weight loss.

He emphasized that lasting success comes from addressing the many factors that influence a person's health and relationship with food.

"I don't think it's ever going to be one thing," Suplee explained. "I think it is partially the amount of food you're consuming, partially the types of food you're consuming, partially how sedentary you are, and partially your emotional and potentially mental behavior and relationship with food."

item.title: Charles Barkley dunks all over pickleball: 'All these old people are killing themselves'
item.description: Charles Barkley calls pickleball 'the gift that keeps giving' for doctors, warning George Kittle about sports injuries plaguing older players.
item.content:encoded:
Former NBA legend Charles Barkley is certainly a very opinionated man, and when he has an opinion, he isn't afraid to let it fly.

The man who once famously said "I am not a role model" joined "The Kittle Cast" with NFL tight end George Kittle and his wife, Claire, and was giving out some rather sage advice about aging athletically.

For guys like Kittle and Barkley, going from the top of your game to retirement can be rough; it can feel like there's a hole in your life where your passion used to be.

That's why Sir Charles felt it paramount to impart his wisdom onto the younger Kittle now so he knows what to expect when he does decide to hang it up.

For Chuck, there is a list of dos and don'ts when it comes to staying in shape post-retirement, and while sharing this with the podcast power couple, he decided to take a shot at a very popular sport among retirees.

"There’s not a lot you can do when you get old," Barkley said. "You can’t go play basketball.

"And let me tell you something. They got this stupid thing going around called pickleball, which is the way old people out here are getting hurt all the time."

So, the Round Mound of Rebound is not a big pickleball fan? Got it.

But he continues.

"My doctor friends said pickleball is the gift that keeps giving," Barkley claims. "Because all these old people are killing themselves and hurt all the time. My doctor friends are in heaven right now."

Kittle chimes in and says he's heard similar things about America's fastest-growing sport among the 55-and-over community, citing torn ACLs and broken wrists galore.

"I am never stepping on that damn court," Kittle exclaimed.

I have to say, as someone who was conscripted into the pickleball cult back in 2023 and having "left the reservation," I couldn't agree more.

I was 30 years old thinking this was going to be some relaxing way to spend my weekends as a recently married guy trying to find a hobby, and I could not have been more wrong.

The word "cutthroat" is an understatement.

I was going up against guys (and girls) who were playing this sport as if it was the fifth set of the Australian Open Finals, and the funniest part of all of it was that most of these people were my age or slightly younger.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: Mamdani's faux African accent as telling as it is bizarre
item.description: A resurfaced 2016 video shows Zohran Mamdani speaking in a full African/South Asian accent while promoting a Disney film he worked on as a dance adviser.
item.content:encoded:
In a resurfaced 2016 interview, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks for the entire time in an African/South Asian accent that sounds like a mix between Trevor Noah and Apu from "The Simpsons." It is absolutely bizarre, but it is also telling.

At the time, he was promoting a Disney movie that he had worked on as a dance adviser, one of the few actual jobs hizzoner has ever held. His signature smile is on display, but when he opens his lips he sounds like someone we have never heard.

With his sing-songy affected voice he decries how in Africa everybody dances, but in New York the men "just grind," but don’t dance. It is a performance entirely in character, he even imitates some Bollywood-style dance moves.

FLASHBACK: MAMDANI'S HISTORY OF DODGING QUESTIONS ABOUT WHERE HE STANDS ON KEY ISSUES

This is not Hillary Clinton’s voice getting a bit twangly when she speaks in the South. This is a full-on acting job, and further proof that the theater kids have taken over the American Left.

There is nothing inherently wrong with theater kids. I myself plied the boards in New York for many years before my career in journalism. But I never did an entire interview with a fake accent as if it was how I actually spoke, and neither did anyone else I know.

Because that is simply downright bizarre behavior.

This is not the first time we have seen different versions of Mamdani that seem like entirely different people. We have also seen him furious and screaming while protesting against ICE in a way that is entirely antithetical to the calm, never flustered, smiley character he plays now, as mayor.

TOM HOMAN WARNS ICE SURGE COMING TO NEW YORK CITY AS MAMDANI BOASTS ABOUT SANCTUARY STATUS

Mamdani’s defenders say that he is merely "code-switching," and that so-called marginalized people will subconsciously speak one way with their own group and another way outside of it. Sorry, but this accent was so perfected and performative that there is zero chance he didn’t know he was doing it.

It does raise an interesting question though: Is the African accent how Zany Zohran really talks, behind closed doors? Could it be his American accent that is the performance? We can’t really know.

In a way, this goofy accent incident is a good metaphor for Democratic Socialism writ large. For outside audiences, they speak in Americanized, vague terms about helping the working class, but you get these same people on a private Zoom call and it's blood and guts communism all the way down.

How many times have we heard "Oh, they aren’t really socialists, they are Democratic Socialists," as if there is one scintilla of difference once they start talking about abolishing the Senate, controlling the housing market and seizing the means of production?

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

One does have to admit, though, that the casting directors at the DSA hit the ball out of the park with Zohran. His fake plastic smile is the pitch-perfect mask for his Marxism. But who really lies underneath? The African choreographer? The furious protester? All of them?

The overwhelming sense one gets with these DSA candidates, like Mamdani, and Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, is that they are carefully curating just how radical they can appear to be to normal, everyday Americans, while their diehard supporters are in on the joke.

This was on display at El-Sayed’s victory party, last week, when he and podcasting antisemite Hasan Piker were talking to a supporter who told them, "People are stupid. This politics of no translation is going to be the way forward, money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all. No one has to decipher what that means." Piker and El-Sayed both appeared in agreement.

Mamdani and the DSA have proven that they will adopt any accent, don any garb, and utter any platitude to get the only thing that they really want, which is power over our lives.

The problem for New Yorkers and Americans is that we can have no idea what really lies beneath the many masks of Mamdani, whether he is the calm smiley American guy, the frothing lunatic protester, or the goofy African choreographer.

In fact, it seems like Mamdani is simply whoever he thinks you want him to be at any given moment. But it's getting old. As his budget numbers fail to line up and rents keep soaring, Gotham needs a leader, not a character actor.

Please, Mr. Mayor, we are all asking you, will the real Mamdani please stand up?

item.content:encoded:
The tensions between the far-left and more establishment wings of the Democratic Party are not going away, as evidenced by some sharp comments from former presidential nominee Hillary Clinton this week.

Clinton lamented during a Friday interview that the far-left doesn’t fall in line and support establishment Democrats as figures like Hasan Piker are demanding fealty, while also warning Republican attacks on hard-left socialists could be "very effective."

"Pivot" podcast host Kara Swisher noted to Clinton that the Democratic Party is having a tense internal struggle between its more establishment and progressive wings to the point that Republican opposition has learned to capitalize on it.

"I think there's no doubt that, you know, the Republican Party is the Trump cult and the Democratic Party is a bigger tent. You know, we do have a broad cross-section of people, what they believe, what their experiences are. I think that's an advantage," Clinton said. "But we also have to win general elections."

Clinton noted that many Democrats now will have to learn to pivot and support the progressive Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign to defeat Republican Mike Rogers, while El-Sayed’s supporters will have to learn how to re-integrate defeated Haley Stevens and her supporters who they were "vilifying" online and in person.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Clinton warned that the Democratic Party’s coalition cannot afford to keep being a one-way street in terms of supporting candidates.

"One thing that we haven't yet seen enough of is that when the progressives, the left — whatever we want to call, you know, candidates on that side of the Democratic Party — when they lose, they often don't support the candidate that has been nominated," she said. "You know, there was a lot of reluctance to support Kamala Harris. There was a lot of reluctance to support me when I got the nomination. So, it can't be a one-way street."

"If we're going to have a fair election, as there was in Michigan, and somebody comes out ahead, a little bit ahead, but needs to get a huge percentage of the voters that voted for Haley, they're going to have to be willing to, you know, get in — get into a conversation that brings those people over," she added, noting that the real struggle will be persuading independents and Stevens supporters.

Clinton warned again that when moderates pivot to support progressive nominees, the progressive nominee needs to make sure that those moderates feel welcomed, adding, "Look, we’ve got to work together. We're not going to beat Republicans by being divided."

James Carville, who helped mastermind Bill Clinton's 1992 election victory, told Fox News Digital this week that the 2028 primary would be a true test of the strength of the far-left in the party. Carville has warned that he could leave the party if it makes room for extreme figures like Piker, who campaigned with El-Sayed.

item.title: Controversial streamer Hasan Piker's lecture axed by University of Washington amid free-speech questions
item.description: Hasan Piker's canceled University of Washington lecture sparks a free speech debate as FIRE questions whether public backlash drove the decision.
item.content:encoded:
A University of Washington lecture featuring progressive Twitch commentator Hasan Piker is off, with school officials citing a flawed planning process as the reason for the cancellation.

Piker, a far-left streamer and YouTube personality, was set to appear in January as part of the school’s 2026-27 Speaker Series, the university said in a statement.

However, following "a review of the process by which the event was planned," the university canceled the event.

MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER

"It was determined that the process for organizing this event did not meet the necessary level of rigor for University-hosted events in the Speaker Series," the statement said.

"Going forward, procedures will be updated to ensure the standards we have for University-hosted events like the Speaker Series are met, particularly so that we can help elevate the level of dialogue on divisive topics during a polarized time in our country," it added.

The university’s cancellation of Piker, who previously said America "deserved 9/11" before later calling the remark "inappropriate," has prompted criticism from First Amendment advocates, with the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) condemning the move.

"If the decision was based on process — and not public backlash or criticism — @UW should be transparent about what standards were not met and how they were applied," the organization said in an X post.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

"Public universities can set standards for events. But they can’t use those standards as cover for canceling a speaker because of their views," it added.

Andrew Kolvet, the executive producer of the Charlie Kirk Show and a Turning Point USA spokesperson, said on X: "Let the radical Mao loving communist Hasan Piker speak, so long as he can resist the urge to call for the death of his political opponents. Universities do this to TPUSA often and blame some admin error etc. It’s wrong." 

Piker, a socialist, rose to fame following a series of controversial comments, and most recently faced backlash after he called for Democrats who are unsupportive of Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to face consequences for not holding the party line.

The popular streamer added that the party should use "Marxist-Leninist" punishment against anyone who fails to "follow the party line," but acknowledged that debate among the Democrats is expected in order to reach a decision.

HASAN PIKER CALLS FOR DEMOCRATS WHO OPPOSE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO BE 'PUNISHED'

His comments came just two days after El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, narrowly defeating Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the primary. Piker had previously appeared alongside El-Sayed on the campaign trail, who is set to face off against Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November.

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville, who has previously spoken out against Piker’s rhetoric, recently doubled down on his criticism of the podcaster.

"I am not going to be in the same party with Hasan Piker," Carville said on "The Sunday Briefing" earlier this month. "If he becomes a force in a Democratic Party, I'm out of here. I have no intention of ever being in the same political party with that guy."

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Carville said that the Democrats will have to decide in the 2028 primary which direction it is headed in, as Piker’s viewpoints become more prevalent within the party.

FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES'

"Everyone claims they're the ascendant ring, alright, on the 2028 presidential election, and this can only be resolved at the presidential level. It cannot be resolved at the state level," Carville told Fox News Digital. "And I am sure that there will be robust representation from the DSA ring of the party, whatever you want to call it. I'm sure there'll be a robust number of candidates from what I would call the governing wing of the Democratic Party, but you call it what you want."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Washington and Piker for comment.

Fox News Digital’s Alexander Hall and Rachel Wolf contributed to this report.

item.title: Nigeria's largest rescue operation frees 308 hostages held by militants in Kwara State
item.description: Victims of a six-month jihadi kidnapping in Nigeria's Kwara State describe starvation, forced births, and burying fellow captives in a forest hideout.
item.content:encoded:
Victims held for six months in captivity at the hands of jihadi kidnappers in Nigeria detailed on Friday the harrowing conditions they were kept in after being liberated in what Nigerian officials are calling the largest rescue operation in the country's history.

Nigerian forces rescued at least 308 victims from captivity in the past week, with the bulk of the victims coming from two distinct groups. 163 of the victims were taken from the Woro community in Nigeria's Kwara State in a Feb. 3 raid that saw their jihadi kidnappers kill an additional 160 people in the Woro village.

The victims told the Associated Press that they believed they had been taken as punishment for refusing to accept and acquiesce to the religious preachings of the jihadis.

One woman, Hauwa Saliu, told the outlet that her captors constantly asked the victims if they had accepted jihad yet.

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

"We prayed to God to help us go back home, but it never really crossed our minds that we were going to go back home," she told the outlet.

Another victim, Amira Saliu, described the conditions in which the women and children were being kept, explaining that they were held in a forest near a river, and forced to put out fires and hide when they heard helicopters nearby.

FREED HOSTAGE ROM BRASLAVSKI DETAILS ABUSE, STARVATION DURING 738 DAYS IN GAZA CAPTIVITY

Saliu, a nurse, also explained how she had to help 10 women give birth with no medical equipment or sanitary gloves.

"I had no choice but to use my bare hands," she told the outlet.

Mary Ishaya, 44, told the outlet that the captives often went days without food and had to bury other captives who had died.

"I still cannot find the right words to describe what has happened to us. We saw death and suffering," she said.

The governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRasaq, told reporters during a news conference that 46 victims were being treated at a hospital.

"This is indeed, indeed a very sad situation. We've not yet come to terms with it. We're still assessing the situation. As you can see, it's just kids ... children and women that are here today," he said. "It's truly a shame that this has happened."

COULD THIS AFRICAN NATION BECOME TRUMP'S NEXT TERROR TARGET AS JIHADISTS CLOSE IN ON POWER?

The incident highlights the ongoing tensions between Nigeria's militant Islamic insurgency in the north and the country's large Christian population, who make up roughly 45% of Nigeria's citizens.

On Christmas Day, President Donald Trump, in coordination with Nigeria's government, authorized precision missile strikes on Islamic State-affiliated groups in northern Nigeria, citing the need to protect the country's Christians.

The U.S. followed up in May, launching coordinated joint military action that reportedly resulted in the death of senior Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Mainuk.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: 'DEI queen': Virginia Dem's past embrace of far-left prosecutors unearthed
item.description: Shannon Taylor's record as Henrico County prosecutor clashes with her tough-on-crime campaign image as she seeks Virginia's 1st congressional district.
item.content:encoded:
Shannon Taylor, now the Democratic nominee in the race for Virginia’s First Congressional district, once endorsed progressive prosecutorial blueprints, advocating for less incarceration and more diversity as a Henrico County commonwealth attorney — some of the same "Democratic values" that ended in tragedy in other parts of Virginia.

Shortly after coming into the role in 2012, Taylor fired seven prosecutors under her.

"I stated publicly that the office needs to have more diversity and I’m going to keep to that public statement," Taylor said in an interview ahead of the firings.

Her track record is sparking criticism that she used her role to prioritize ideological and political views at the expense of public safety. It’s also clashing with portrayals from her campaign, highlighting her work as a tough-on-crime figure as she looks to win over a Republican-leaning district.

FORMER PROSECUTOR WHO ACCUSED TRUMP OF WEAPONIZING DOJ WINS DEM PRIMARY

Taylor highlighted her work as she topped a crowded field of Democratic candidates vying to challenge Republican incumbent Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Va.

"As Henrico’s top prosecutor for the last 14 years, Shannon has tried thousands of cases and put violent criminals, drug traffickers and abusers behind bars," Taylor states on her campaign website. "She has a record of shutting down fraudsters trying to take advantage of working families and locking up violent criminals who threaten our safety."

But that hasn’t always been the appearance she’s given.

After her seven firings, Taylor faced blowback for trying to hire a woman named Misty Whitehead as a police oversight prosecutor. However, before the role could be made official, social media posts from Whitehead surfaced that seemingly showed a pattern of attacking police.

Taylor faced backlash from the town’s county manager over her selected candidate.

"A county manager can’t tell a commonwealth’s attorney who to hire, but he can recommend whether or not local funds are included to supplement that salary. And in this case, I absolutely will not do it under any circumstances," County Manager John Vithoulkas said at the time.

Whitehead had a history of voicing concerns about police behavior and social justice that raised concerns for at least one county official, according to local reports.

Taylor defended her pick, telling local outlets that she believed the posts were "thoughtful analysis of the current events we are all living through."

Taylor also has ties to similarly-minded prosecutors in other counties — some of which entered the public eye recently due to tragic circumstances.

SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS

In Fairfax County, Virginia, news broke that Abdul Jalloh, a 32-year-old illegal alien from Sierra Leone, stabbed a Virginia resident to death at a bus stop despite over 30 prior arrests and a known tendency for violent behavior.

Jalloh’s criminal record included charges of rape, malicious wounding, assault, drug possession, identity theft, trespassing, larceny and firing a weapon.

Even so, prosecutor Steve Descano had dropped many of them, prompting concern and outrage from lawmakers.

"You dismissed the case, and it’s shameful," Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C. said at a hearing where Descano was summoned to Congress to explain a series of similar cases.

Knott had been highlighting one such instance involving a child predator.

"When you dismiss a case, what happens to that defendant? He walks free. A disgusting, perverted individual preying on children, that you dismissed," Knott said.

Long before Descano’s time in the spotlight, Taylor had endorsed Descano, supporting his bid to become county prosecutor in 2019, citing shared outlooks.

"I am excited to endorse Steve Descano for Fairfax County’s Commonwealth’s Attorney because I know he will prioritize the same Democratic values we all share, making Fairfax a safe and just place for everyone and I am looking forward to working with him," Taylor wrote.

Taylor and Descano would go on to champion their shared values in a 2021 letter to the Biden Administration.

In it, the two joined 100 other district and county attorneys in championing a set of "21 principles for the 21st-Century prosecutor." The authors claimed that "tough on crime policies" had been "anathema to justice," championed an end to mandatory minimums and three-strike laws, advocated for taking immigration status into consideration when negotiating sentences and plea deals, and opposed calling rapists "rapists," drug dealers "drug dealers," and convicted criminals "felons" or "inmates."

"A number of elected reform-minded prosecutors are boldly redefining what it means to be a prosecutor," the letter states.

OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’

At least one Republican onlooker blasted Taylor’s record.

"She spent her time reshaping the prosecutor's office around identity politics, pushing a far-left agenda that put woke activism ahead of public safety, and fighting to turn Virginia into a far-left hellscape," Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Instead of prosecuting criminals and making Virginia safer, DEI queen Shannon Taylor chose to be a diversity, equity, and inclusion consultant."

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Taylor now heads to the general election on Nov. 3. Wittman, the district’s incumbent, last won re-election in 2024 in a 56.3% to 43.5% victory over Democratic challenger Leslie Mehta, an attorney.

item.title: Lawyer-turned-social media sensation is betting it all on God, love and grief
item.description: With a book deal and international tour ahead, Davide De Pierro explains how his car vlogs and Italian-American roots helped him earn 6 million followers — and growing.
item.content:encoded:
In a digital landscape often dominated by outrage, carefully curated perfection and fleeting trends, Davide De Pierro has built an audience by doing something refreshingly simple: telling honest stories about his experiences that make people feel seen. The New Jersey attorney-turned-digital creator joined Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview to discuss why authenticity — not algorithms — has become his greatest asset in a world where millions of people (six million who follow De Pierro, to be exact) are still searching for genuine human connection.

The 38-year-old was born in New Jersey and spent his early years in Italy before returning to Jersey City, where he still lives today. Though he continues to practice law at a family firm with his father and brother in Bloomfield, his career took a turn when he found success on TikTok and Instagram — pulling viewers in with his sometimes sarcastic, always profound reflections on work, life, love and faith.

"Being a person has been the same, always. What's changed is what you're wearing and what technology you're using," De Pierro said. "But really, I'm just talking about the human condition."

The self-described "half Italian/half Jersey boy" is now poised to re-release his self-published audiobook with HarperCollins in both a new audio edition and a hardcover version. The novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," will also heavily feature in his upcoming international tour, which will include stand-up comedy, live readings of excerpts from his book, a Q&A session and a meet-and-greet.

De Pierro is best known for his single-shot vlogs taken in his car, branded with captions like, "If I saw an alien I wouldn't even care honestly I got too much going on right now," "Started using my own money and realized my mom was right, we do have food at home," and "No matter what I have God."

On the heels of his life-changing success, De Pierro has remained humble — in fact, when asked what he believed made him so popular on social media, he found himself at a loss for words.

CANCEL ME IF YOU CAN: DAVE PORTNOY TAKES AIM AT CANCEL CULTURE CRITICS WHO 'ALREADY DECIDED' THE VERDICT

"I don't know why people are following me. I mean, I know what I do. I go on there and I talk about stuff. And maybe it's, in part, it could be the delivery. In part, it could be the actual language. In part, it could be the way my face looks in the car. I don't know. But I think it just happened."

"I'm happy that I won this little social media lottery, because otherwise I wouldn't be able to put my book out there and go on tour and meet people and have fun. And I'd be stuck in the law office all the time... Now I have to leave for other reasons, so my father permits me to go out and do a tour," he joked.

The creator described his success as "accidental" and said there was no "influencer strategy." Ironically, he used to consider himself "chronically offline."

"I was 37 years old. So, you know, I felt like that ship had sailed. I wasn't going to go dance on TikTok. Probably not for the best."

He credited an ex-girlfriend with the initial idea of posting his reflections on the internet.

"I thought that was a ridiculous idea. But I eventually took her advice, especially after the breakup — that's when men always take all the good advice from their exes. And it worked. And it kept working."

Millennials — the generation to which De Pierro proudly belongs — have been experiencing burnout for years, with research reported from Gallup to even the National Institutes of Health supporting the claim.

De Pierro told Fox News Digital he often posts about "workplace malaise," dating fatigue, and other kinds of exhaustion because he finds it's not just relatable, it's real.

"I think that you can't fake the authenticity of exhaustion. I think the relatability is that it's real. And so I am a person who has worked and who has gone through relationship problems. I'm not an inexperienced, younger man who's just kind of making things up that might be relatable. And I guess you just can't fabricate that kind of authenticity," said De Pierro, musing on how what some might call his late arrival to social media makes him stand out from other career influencers.

"The authenticity is not special, this isn't unique to me. I'm just describing what we all go through, but you have to go through it first. And so, certainly, there is an advantage to being a content creator in your late 30s if you're going to be talking about the struggles of being alive."

The TikToker pointed to the prolific nature and timelessness of William Shakespeare as an example of connection.

"What does he have in common with me, a 15th century English guy?" he posited in the wide-ranging interview. "In reality, he has everything in common with you, because he's a human being."

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

De Pierro's own audience is further evidence of this hypothesis, he said.

"My following is really a social experiment, if you look at it. I mean, there are people from all over the world and on all different spectrums. And I wonder if they know that they're following the same person, because I'm just talking about being a person. And everyone can relate to the experiences that we all go through every day, which are universal."

As a working attorney, De Pierro made it clear that his online ponderings should not be taken as legal advice.

"I would never call what I'm doing online advice. Especially being a lawyer, I'm so afraid of the word ‘advice.’ We never advise you unless you are our client."

"I don't want people to listen to it as advice. I'm not an expert on anything. I'm sharing observations, sharing experiences, sharing thoughts, but certainly not advice. No, don't do anything I say," he joked.

VIRAL BOY BAND INSISTS IT'S REAL AS IMMIGRATION FIGHT PUTS INTERNET FAME TO GOVERNMENT TEST

He attributed his contemplative style more to his Italian-American heritage than to his career in law, labeling Italians as "natural storytellers" and "expert complainers."

"I think it's part of the Italian identity to be a little bit playfully pessimistic. There might be even a superstition in that. You don't want to assume success."

"And so, I think that that plays into my character and my personality even in my videos. There's an exhaustion, there's a playful sense of pessimism there sometimes. A negativity almost. But it hides a more profound, I think, joy and optimism that Italians do have."

Despite referring to his portrayal in his social media videos as a "character," De Pierro told Fox News Digital that in the age-old Instagram vs. Reality — a concept that contrasts real-life with people's online personas — the lawyer-turned-comedian remains authentically himself.

"I mean, we all contain multitudes, right? So I think one of my personalities involves what I do in the car... All these little accents and modes of speaking are real to me. It depends on who I'm with. If I'm with my Jersey City friends, it's going to sound like "Goodfellas." But if I'm in a court of law, then I have to rein in it a little bit."

Add professional code-switcher to his growing list of accolades. 

Despite often baring his soul online, De Pierro said sharing his thoughts for all the world to see hasn't affected his personal life much — yet.

"It is real, it is authentic, and so it doesn't affect my life because I'm already being myself on camera. So it's not like I'm suddenly unrecognizable to my friends and family, they know that guy intimately," De Pierro maintained.

"But on the other hand — I'm not dating much — but I suspect that it will affect my dating, because I think people are starting to get the impression that I'm this enlightened man, and maybe they're going to have expectations of me in dating that are unrealistic.

"I'm just as much of an idiot as the men that I talk about in my videos."

JEFF FOXWORTHY PULLS BACK THE CURTAIN ON COMEDY'S CREATIVE PROCESS FOR WHAT COULD BE HIS LAST SPECIAL

It is always easier to give advice than to take it, he added.

"I'm still a person. And also, by the way, that wisdom is for everyone else. I'm just good at giving other people advice as opposed to living it myself. I've always been that friend that's really good at telling you what's wrong with you. But if I have to apply it to my own life, I'm probably going to fail nine times out of ten."

For someone who speaks openly about relationships and the roller coaster of emotions they bring, the Heartbreak Heartthrob reveals relatively little about the concrete details of his private life. 

That's intentional.

"What's funny about all this is that I'm incredibly public in the sense that I am constantly sharing my thoughts, but I'm almost never sharing my life. I'm just in the car. No one knows where I live. No one's ever seen my family. No one has ever seen the lower half of my body. So I'm extremely private while at the same time having a therapy session in my car," De Pierro told Fox News Digital.

De Pierro now speaks openly about many subjects with his growing following, but there is one he had to work his way up to: his faith.

He told Fox News Digital he is "100%" a Christian man, having gone to church every Sunday with his family all his life.

"My faith plays a huge role in my personal life. And so it was just a natural transition for me. As soon as I saw that I had this following and this kind of engagement, I thought, 'Wow, this is a perfect opportunity to speak about something that's really important to me.'"

De Pierro was inspired by the story of his grandfather, who died shortly after De Pierro was born.

FROM ‘SCREAM’ TO STREAM: JAMIE KENNEDY REVEALS HOW HOLLYWOOD LOST ITS WAY AND WHY HE WON'T GIVE UP ON LA

"He was a preacher, and apparently — at least from the stories I've been told — a beloved man in the very small community that he lived and worked in. And a part of me thought, 'Here was this incredible man that I never met who only was able to speak to a few hundred people, maybe a thousand, over the course of his life.'"

"So I saw the opportunity that I had, and I thought to myself, 'Here I am, not even a tenth of the man that my grandfather was. And I have the opportunity to speak to millions of people at times. I have to use this opportunity, even if I could just plant a little seed of faith in these invisible people that are watching me from wherever they may be.'"

He has received no shortage of warm messages from viewers saying his posts have touched them and even helped them through hard times.

"And that's gratifying, too, of course, to feel like you're doing something more than just entertaining. Because it's great to get people to laugh and to get to feel seen and understood."

"But if you could also help people in a way that, again — it sounds crazy to me. I mean, I don't think that anything I'm doing is particularly helpful. But when I see those messages, I believe them. If they felt that way, then it's gratifying to know that I'm doing something, hopefully, useful."

HarperCollins imprint Hanover Square Press announced Monday it is set to publish De Pierro's debut novel, "The Letters I Never Sent," now on pre-sale and set for print and ebook publication on December 8, 2026. The audiobook version, De Pierro told FOX, will be available this October. Additionally, he will embark on his first-ever stand-up tour beginning late September.

The writer, performer, and viral content creator also shared his biggest icks and ticks, what he really thinks of modern dating, and the best advice he's ever received with Fox News Digital. But when asked if he had one final message he'd want to leave behind for his followers, it's a sentiment as refreshingly simple as he is: "God loves you."

item.title: Carmen Electra says 'Baywatch' pushed boundaries without crossing the line: 'It wasn't porn'
item.description: Carmen Electra reveals what made the original "Baywatch" a global phenomenon while promoting the new competition show, "Nation's Dumbest" on Fox.
item.content:encoded:
Carmen Electra is reminiscing about her days starring in the original "Baywatch."

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant discussed the success of the original series, saying, all "the cast members made it special."

"It's hard to replace Pamela [Anderson] and Yasmine [Bleeth] and all those people. And there was just a certain tone. I don't know how to explain it," she said. "It had a certain tone to it that it was just such a fantasy, and maybe it was the first time on television you could see so much skin because we really were playing lifeguards right so we could be in these skimpy outfits."

She went on to say that the show possibly left people thinking, "Oh my God, what is this? We can see nipples."

BROOKS NADER SIZZLES IN ICONIC RED SWIMSUIT AS SHE SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES SNAPS FROM 'BAYWATCH' REBOOT SET

"And it wasn't porn. You know, what I mean? They didn't have to sneak away and find a VHS tape to like, sneak and put in. You can watch this," she added. "You can also learn something. Because, we heard from a lot of people, a lot of fans out there, that they learned so much watching the show."

Electra credited the show's sexy nature as one of the reasons it became the global phenomenon it is, saying they were "sometimes trying to be sexy, sometimes not trying to be sexy" and that "all of a sudden, you get these guys on there with these gorgeous bodies."

In addition to the sexy aspect of the show, Electra attributed its success to the fact that fans could learn something from the show, including how to give CPR, adding she also "learned how to give CPR," and joked, "I could save someone right now if I needed to."

The actress and model joined the show in 1997 for its eighth season, after gaining exposure from posing for Playboy in a 1996 pictorial.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In terms of returning for the new reboot of the series, Electra is open to putting on the iconic red one-piece once again, since her former love interest on the show, David Chokachi has signed on to return.

"I could do something. Come in, have another love scene with David Chokachi. Just something really cute and fun. I would be down to get into the water again," she said. "I think it would be fun it makes sense I was David Chokachi's love interest way back then. I think it would be really fun and why not, you know?"

His character, Cody Madison, is now the owner of a beachside bar, The Shoreline, and also acts as a mentor to the younger new lifeguards.

"I think it would be so cool if I just came in for an episode to surprise him and say hi. They fall in love again, who knows," Electra said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

One thing the actress is not willing to go through again is "the schooling that I did when I first joined the cast," noting, "that was really tough."

Following her time on "Baywatch," Electra had a successful career in both film and television, appearing in films such as "Scary Movie," "Cheaper by the Dozen 2," "Meet the Spartans" and others.

She also recently appeared as a contestant on "Nation's Dumbest," a new celebrity competition show. She told Fox News Digital she originally didn't want to do it, saying, "I didn't pay attention in school" and that she "didn't have a good feeling about it."

"Fox kept getting on the phone. They're like, it's gonna be so easy. It's gonna be fun. It's like acting think of it as an acting role," she said. "Once I was not there anymore, I kind of missed it...and there was a lot of fun. I did miss the cast a lot but yeah, I think we were all sitting there going, 'What? Why the hell did we subject ourselves to be on this show?'"

"I definitely had a lot of anxiety and I would freeze. As soon as we would have to rush and say something, answer a question really fast or there was something weird we had to do," she added. "It could be very stressful and I would freeze."

When it came to a moment that still haunts her, Electra couldn't believe she couldn't remember what BBL stood for, saying the producers threw in "a really easy question that she's gonna get and I got it wrong. I couldn't believe it."

item.title: Slain California fire captain’s wife admits murder after Mexico capture, serving time for killing first spouse
item.description: Surveillance footage captured Cal Fire captain Rebecca Marodi fleeing before the fatal stabbing at the couple's San Diego County home in Ramona.
item.content:encoded:
A California woman has pleaded guilty to murdering her fire captain spouse last year, decades after she was convicted in the fatal stabbing of her former husband.

Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty Tuesday to second-degree murder in the death of her wife, Rebecca "Becky" Marodi, 49, a longtime California firefighter who was found fatally stabbed at the couple’s Ramona home in February 2025.

When asked by the judge how she pleaded to count 1, second-degree murder, Marodi said, "Guilty."

SLAIN CALIFORNIA FIRE CAPTAIN'S FUGITIVE WIFE ‘SCARED’ EX MOTHER-IN-LAW

As part of the plea, Marodi also admitted to having a prior serious felony conviction stemming from the 2000 stabbing death of her then-husband, James Joseph Olejniczak.

She pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter in that case in 2003 before her release in 2013, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Rebecca Marodi, a veteran Cal Fire captain, suffered multiple stab wounds during the Feb. 17, 2025 attack.

Prosecutors said surveillance footage captured her fleeing the home as Yolanda Marodi pursued her. Rebecca was found with several injuries to her neck, chest and back that authorities said were consistent with a stabbing.

Investigators later alleged that Marodi fled to Mexico after the killing, where she remained for more than a month before being arrested in Mexicali and returned to the United States.
